claim: The Scott-Knott effect size difference test is the test this source introduces (attribution of the method).
quote:
Furthermore, we introduce (4) the Scott-Knott Effect Size
Difference (ESD) test—an enhancement of the standard
Scott-Knott test (which cluster distributions into statistically
distinct ranks [90])
locator: p. 2 (printed = PDF), Sec. 1; defined Sec. 5.8.1, pp. 8-9
issue: Attribution holds. The source also cites its own earlier R package (ref. [104], 2015) for the implementation, but the paper claims the introduction, so citing it is defensible.

claim: The test applied in the dissertation (ranking MTDs by NCR reduction, groups split only where significant and non-negligible) is the Scott-Knott ESD test as this source defines it.
quote:
The Scott-Knott ESD test will (1) correct the non-
normal distribution of an input dataset; and (2) merge any
two statistically distinct groups that have a negligible effect
size into one group.
Normality Correction. The Scott-Knott test assumes that
the data under analysis are normally distributed. Thus, we
mitigate the skewness by log-transforming each treatment
(lnðx þ 1Þ)
issue: The source's ESD test has two steps: a ln(x+1) normality correction and the negligible-effect merge. The repo implementation (data/results/ch5_defended/sk_esd.py) keeps the Scott-Knott split and the merge but has no log-transform step, and NCR reduction can be negative, where ln(x+1) is undefined below -1. Naming the test bare implies the source's full procedure. The sentence after it ('differ significantly and by more than a negligible effect') matches step 2 and the alpha = 0.05 split.
fix_text: The Scott--Knott effect size difference test \citep{tantithamthavorn2017empirical}, without its log-transform step, ranks the MTD by NCR reduction ...
